rounds.proof_sketch: K=4096, TILE_SIZE=32. Number of tile iterations = (4096+31)/32 = 128. For last tile (t=127), B_row = 127*32 + ty ∈ [4064, 4095]. Maximum B_row = 4095 < K = 4096. The boundary case B_row == K is never reached, so `B_row < K` and `B_row <= K` evaluate identically for all threads.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the boundary check from `B_row < K` to `B_row <= K`. This would only produce a different result when B_row equals exactly K. With fixed shapes A[4096,1024] and B[4096,2048], K=4096 is exactly divisible by TILE_SIZE=32. The loop runs for exactly 128 tiles (t=0..127), and for the last tile (t=127), B_row ranges from 4064 to 4095. Since the maximum B_row (4095) is strictly less than K (4096), the condition `B_row < K` is always true whenever valid indices are accessed, making the mutation semantically equivalent. No value-level test can change this geometric fact determined by the fixed dimensions.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed shape contract. The mutant would only be distinguishable if K were not a multiple of TILE_SIZE (e.g., K=4097), which would cause some threads in the last tile to have B_row=K, triggering out-of-bounds access with the mutant. Since K=4096=128*32, this boundary case is geometrically unreachable.
rounds.recommendations: When testing boundary condition mutations in tiled GPU kernels, verify whether the mutation's distinguishing condition (here B_row==K) is reachable given the fixed dimensions. Mutations in bounds-checking code become unkillable when dimensions are exact multiples of tile sizes. Consider parameterized testing with non-aligned dimensions when kernel correctness for general inputs is important.
